actuator_details: mathematical control framework

actuator_details: Four-legged hydraulic walking machine, 1400 kg dry mass, 1500 kg payload capacity, 5.5m long. Each leg has 3 hydraulic cylinders for rotation/extension/elevation. Driven by 90 hp Continental gasoline engine driving hydraulic pump.
control_architecture: master-slave kinesthetic teleoperation: human operator's arms and legs are strapped into kinesthetic-feedback exoskeleton; force-reflecting servo couples operator joint position/torque to vehicle leg position/torque; operator feels the vehicle's interaction forces
creator: Ralph S. Mosher and team, General Electric Research Laboratory, Schenectady NY
disclosure_citation: Mosher, Ralph S. 'Test and evaluation of a versatile walking truck.' General Electric Schenectady Research Lab Report, September 1968. Published abstract: Mosher, R.S. 'Exploring the potential of a quadruped'. Society of Automotive Engineers, January 1969 (Detroit Engineering Show, Paper 690191).
notable_capabilities: hydraulic legged locomotion at 1500 kg payload
master-slave kinesthetic control with force feedback
prior_art_notes: The GE Walking Truck is the deepest hydraulic legged-locomotion academic disclosure in the corpus and substantially predates everything in the modern legged-robotics commercial portfolio. Mosher's 1968 SAE paper discloses with full specificity: (1) hydraulic actuation per leg with 3-DOF — anticipates hydraulic legged claims by Boston Dynamics (BigDog 2005) by 37 years; (2) master-slave kinesthetic teleoperation with force feedback — anticipates teleoperation claims for legged systems; (3) 1500 kg payload legged loadbearing — anticipates legged-loadbearing claims (Boston Dynamics LS3, Ghost Robotics Vision 60); (4) 90 hp combustion engine power source for legged locomotion. Modern claims on hydraulic / combustion-powered legged loadbearing all face this 1968 disclosure as 102 prior art at unusual depth. Publicly funded research, openly published.
sensing: force feedback at every joint; visual via operator's direct view; no autonomous sensing
sources: Mosher, R.S. 'Exploring the potential of a quadruped'. SAE Paper 690191, 1969.
Mosher, R.S. 'Test and evaluation of a versatile walking truck'. GE Schenectady Research Lab Report, 1968.
Liston, R. and Mosher, R. 'A versatile walking truck'. Mechanical Engineering 90(8): 12-19, 1968.

actuator_details: Single pneumatic-piston leg with hip joint for fore-aft balance; planar (2D) constrained motion. Pneumatic spring leg with active hip-position control. The leg compresses on landing and extends to provide thrust.
control_architecture: three-part decoupled control: (1) hopping height regulated by leg-spring extension during stance; (2) forward velocity regulated by foot-placement during flight; (3) body attitude regulated by hip torque. The decoupling is the disclosure.
creator: Marc H. Raibert; CMU Leg Laboratory, then MIT Leg Laboratory
disclosure_citation: Raibert, Marc H. 'Hopping in legged systems — modeling and simulation for the two-dimensional one-legged case'. IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics SMC-14(3): 451-463, May/June 1984. Earlier: Raibert, M.H. and Brown, H.B. 'Experiments in balance with a 2D one-legged machine'. Trans. ASME, J. Dyn. Sys., Meas., Cont., 106:75-81, 1984.
notable_capabilities: dynamic legged balance via decoupled three-axis control
experimental validation of dynamic legged stability
prior_art_notes: Raibert's hoppers are the foundational academic disclosure of dynamic legged balance and reduced-order-model control. The three-part decoupling (leg height / foot placement / body attitude) is the *exact* control architecture used by every subsequent dynamic-legged academic and commercial system, from Cassie to Atlas to MIT Mini Cheetah. Modern claims on reduced-order-model legged control all face Raibert's 1984 disclosure as 102 prior art. The 1985 book (Legged Robots that Balance, MIT Press) extends the disclosure to 2-legged and 4-legged versions and is one of the most-cited works in legged robotics. Publicly funded research; open publication.
sensing: leg position encoder; body pitch encoder; ground contact sensor
sources: Raibert, M.H. 'Hopping in legged systems'. IEEE Trans. SMC, 1984.
Raibert, M.H. and Brown, H.B. 'Experiments in balance with a 2D one-legged machine'. ASME J. DSMC, 1984.
Raibert, M.H. Legged Robots that Balance. MIT Press, 1986.

actuator_details: Unactuated bipedal mechanism. Knee-locked stance leg + free-swinging swing leg. Hip joint between legs. Walks down a shallow incline on gravity alone, no motors, no batteries, no sensors, no controller.
control_architecture: zero — purely passive mechanical dynamics. The walker's natural limit cycle on a slope produces stable bipedal locomotion. Stability arises from the dynamics, not from feedback.
creator: Tad McGeer, Simon Fraser University
disclosure_citation: McGeer, Tad. 'Passive dynamic walking'. International Journal of Robotics Research 9(2): 62-82, April 1990.
prior_art_notes: The 1990 McGeer disclosure is the foundational academic anchor for energy-efficient bipedal locomotion. Anticipates: (1) the principle that bipedal stability can emerge from passive limb dynamics (with appropriate inertia/length tuning) — directly relevant to modern claims on energy-efficient bipedal control IP; (2) limit-cycle analysis of bipedal gait — anticipates analytical claims on cycle-based gait optimization; (3) the methodological observation that the cost of transport for passive walkers approaches that of human walking. Modern energy-efficient bipedal claims (Cassie, ATRIAS, Berkeley Humanoid) all build on McGeer 1990. Publicly funded research; the 1990 IJRR paper is heavily cited.
sources: McGeer, T. 'Passive dynamic walking'. IJRR 9(2): 62-82, 1990.
Collins, S.H., Wisse, M., Ruina, A. 'A three-dimensional passive-dynamic walking robot with two legs and knees'. IJRR 20(7): 607-615, 2001 (extends McGeer to 3D).

actuator_details: 24-DOF anthropomorphic hand. McKibben-style pneumatic muscles routed antagonistically through tendon channels. Later electric-tendon variants. Compliant fingertip with force sensing; thumb has 5 DOF.
control_architecture: position and force control modes; tendon-tension control via per-actuator solenoids
creator: Shadow Robot Company (Richard Greenhill, Rich Walker, et al.)
disclosure_citation: Greenhill, Richard et al. (Shadow Robot Company). 'Shadow Dexterous Hand'. ICRA workshops 2002 onwards; mechanical disclosures in Greenhill, R., Walker, R. et al. 'The Shadow C5 Hand Prototype'. ICRA Workshop on Humanoid Manipulation, 2007.
end_effector: five-fingered anthropomorphic hand at human scale
prior_art_notes: Shadow's hand is the longest-running academic-grade dexterous hand platform and is the standard reference for tendon-routed anthropomorphic manipulators. Anticipates and provides extensive prior art for: (1) 24-DOF anthropomorphic hand mechanism with separate-finger control — relevant to modern humanoid hand IP; (2) McKibben-style pneumatic muscle actuation in a hand — relevant to artificial-muscle hand claims; (3) tendon-tension control as a viable closed-loop mode for dexterity — relevant to tendon-controlled hand IP. Shadow has published extensively in IEEE proceedings since 2002, and the platform is licensed to academic labs worldwide. Modern Tesla, Figure, and 1X hand patents face Shadow's 22+ years of accumulated public disclosure.
sensing: strain gauges in tendon paths; fingertip pressure sensors; joint encoders
sources: Shadow Robot Company. 'Shadow C5 Hand'. ICRA Workshop on Humanoid Manipulation, 2007.
Shadow Robot Company. Shadow Dexterous Hand technical specification (publicly distributed).

actuator_details: Four-fingered hand, 13 DOF (3 per finger + 1 palm rotation). Brushless DC motors with harmonic-drive reducers. Cable-tendon transmission to phalanges. Joint torque sensing at every actuated joint. Force-torque sensor at fingertip.
control_architecture: impedance control via measured joint torques; backdrivable; supports Cartesian and joint-space control modes
creator: Butterfass, Grebenstein, Liu, Hirzinger; DLR Institute of Robotics and Mechatronics, Oberpfaffenhofen, Germany
disclosure_citation: Butterfass, J., Grebenstein, M., Liu, H., Hirzinger, G. 'DLR-Hand II: next generation of a dextrous robot hand'. IEEE ICRA, 2001 (early disclosure); Butterfass, J. et al. 'Design and Experiences with DLR Hand II'. World Automation Congress, 2004.
end_effector: four-fingered hand with thumb opposition; human-equivalent grasp envelope
notable_capabilities: compact integration of motors+sensors per joint
prior_art_notes: DLR Hand-II is the canonical academic disclosure of joint-torque-sensing dexterous hands with compact actuator integration. Anticipates: (1) impedance-controlled dexterous manipulation with proprioceptive sensing — directly relevant to claims on torque-controlled humanoid hands (every modern humanoid hand IP); (2) cable-tendon transmission with harmonic-drive primary reducer — relevant to combined-mechanism actuator claims; (3) per-joint integrated torque sensor with calibrated absolute position — anticipates proprioceptive-actuator IP. The DLR series (Hand-II, then Hand-III, then Hand Arm System) is one of the deepest academic technical lineages in dexterous manipulation. Continuously published in IEEE proceedings since 2001.
sensing: joint torque sensors at every joint; six-axis force-torque at fingertip; joint position encoders; absolute calibration via Hall sensors
sources: Butterfass, J. et al. 'DLR-Hand II: next generation of a dextrous robot hand'. IEEE ICRA 2001.
Butterfass, J. et al. 'Design and Experiences with DLR Hand II'. World Automation Congress 2004.

actuator_details: Wheeled humanoid: omnidirectional 4-wheel base with variable wheel-base width for stability/agility tradeoff. Two DLR LWR (Light Weight Robot) arms (7 DOF each). Two DLR Hand-II four-finger hands. Sensorized head with stereo cameras and structured light.
control_architecture: impedance control on the arms; coordinated whole-body motion planning; mobile manipulation tasks (catching balls, pouring, two-arm manipulation)
creator: Borst, Wimboeck, Schmidt, Fuchs, Brunner, Zacharias, Giordano, Konietschke, Sepp, Fuchs, Rink, Albu-Schäffer, Hirzinger; DLR Institute of Robotics and Mechatronics
disclosure_citation: Borst, C., Wimboeck, T., Schmidt, F., Fuchs, M., Brunner, B., Zacharias, F., Giordano, P. R., Konietschke, R., Sepp, W., Fuchs, S., Rink, C., Albu-Schäffer, A., Hirzinger, G. 'Rollin' Justin — Mobile platform with variable base'. IEEE ICRA, May 2009.
end_effector: two DLR Hand-II four-finger hands, 12 DOF each
prior_art_notes: Justin is the canonical academic disclosure of wheeled humanoid mobile manipulation with full impedance control. Anticipates and provides extensive prior art for: (1) wheeled humanoid platform for service tasks — relevant to claims on wheeled humanoid IP (Diligent Moxi, NEXTAGE follow this paradigm); (2) torque-controlled dual-arm coordination — relevant to bimanual humanoid manipulation IP; (3) variable-wheelbase mobile base — relevant to morphology-changing wheeled platform claims. DLR has published Justin disclosures in ICRA, IROS, Humanoids continuously since 2009. Modern wheeled humanoid claims face this deep academic anchor.
sensing: stereo cameras, structured light; per-joint torque sensing on arms and hands; force-torque on fingertips
sources: Borst, C. et al. 'Rollin' Justin'. IEEE ICRA 2009.
Bäuml, B. et al. 'Catching flying balls and preparing coffee: humanoid Rollin' Justin performs dynamic and sensitive tasks'. IEEE ICRA 2011.

actuator_details: Torque-controlled bipedal humanoid based on the DLR LWR-III joint design: brushless DC motors with harmonic-drive primary reducers, integrated torque sensors at every joint. Cycloidal-style high-load joints in the legs.
control_architecture: whole-body torque control via passivity-based controllers; divergent component of motion (DCM) for walking; impedance control for whole-body interaction
creator: Englsberger, Werner, Ott, Henze, Roa, Garofalo, Burger, Beyer, Eiberger, Schmid, Albu-Schäffer; DLR Institute of Robotics and Mechatronics
disclosure_citation: Englsberger, J., Werner, A., Ott, C., Henze, B., Roa, M.A., Garofalo, G., Burger, R., Beyer, A., Eiberger, O., Schmid, K., Albu-Schäffer, A. 'Overview of the torque-controlled humanoid robot TORO'. IEEE-RAS Humanoids, July 2014.
prior_art_notes: TORO is the canonical academic disclosure of full-body torque-controlled bipedal humanoid with DCM (Divergent Component of Motion) walking control. Anticipates: (1) torque-controlled whole-body bipedal walking — directly relevant to claims on whole-body torque-controlled humanoid platforms; (2) DCM walking as an alternative to ZMP — relevant to walking-control IP; (3) impedance-control whole-body interaction with humans — relevant to safe-human-interaction humanoid claims. DLR's Englsberger paper introduced the DCM formulation that subsequent humanoids (HRP-5P, several private platforms) adopted. Publicly funded research with extensive IEEE-proceedings publication.
sensing: per-joint torque sensors; joint position encoders; IMU; force-torque at the feet
sources: Englsberger, J. et al. 'Overview of the torque-controlled humanoid robot TORO'. IEEE Humanoids 2014.
Englsberger, J. et al. 'Three-dimensional bipedal walking control based on Divergent Component of Motion'. IEEE T-RO 31(2): 355-368, 2015.

actuator_details: Single-DOF universal gripper: balloon filled with granular material (coffee grounds, etc.) attached to a vacuum line. Pressing into an object deforms the granular medium around the object's shape; vacuum applied to the balloon jams the granular medium into a rigid shape, capturing the object.
control_architecture: binary state: relaxed (granular flow allowed) vs. jammed (granular medium rigid). Vacuum applied via single solenoid valve.
creator: Eric Brown, Nicholas Rodenberg, John Amend, Annan Mozeika, Erik Steltz, Mitchell R. Zakin, Hod Lipson, Heinrich M. Jaeger; Cornell University and University of Chicago
disclosure_citation: Brown, E., Rodenberg, N., Amend, J., Mozeika, A., Steltz, E., Zakin, M.R., Lipson, H., Jaeger, H.M. 'Universal robotic gripper based on the jamming of granular material'. PNAS 107(44): 18809-18814, October 25, 2010.
notable_capabilities: compliance during approach, rigidity during transport
prior_art_notes: The Cornell jamming gripper introduces granular-jamming as a fundamental new class of robotic gripper. Anticipates: (1) jamming-based universal grippers with single-DOF actuation — relevant to modern claims on universal/adaptive grippers; (2) the principle that compliance during approach and rigidity during grasp can be combined in a single deformable structure — relevant to compliant-grasp IP across the soft robotics field. The 2010 PNAS paper is one of the most-cited soft-robotics papers and has been licensed/extended by Empire Robotics (commercial spinoff) and many academic labs. Modern universal-gripper claims face this 2010 anchor.
sources: Brown, E. et al. 'Universal robotic gripper based on the jamming of granular material'. PNAS 107(44), 2010.
Steltz, E., Mozeika, A. et al. 'JSEL: jamming skin enabled locomotion'. IROS 2009 (precursor disclosure).

actuator_details: Anthropomorphic five-fingered hand with 19 internal DOFs but only one motor — actuation by a single tendon routed through a 'first synergy' postural pattern (PCA-derived from human grasping). Compliant joints with elastic returns. Underactuated: most fingers passively conform to grasp shape.
control_architecture: single-DOF tendon position control along the principal grasping synergy; passive compliance handles object shape variation
creator: Catalano, Grioli, Farnioli, Serio, Piazza, Bicchi; Centro 'E. Piaggio', Università di Pisa, and Italian Institute of Technology
disclosure_citation: Catalano, M.G., Grioli, G., Farnioli, E., Serio, A., Piazza, C., Bicchi, A. 'Adaptive synergies for the design and control of the Pisa/IIT SoftHand'. International Journal of Robotics Research 33(5): 768-782, November 3, 2014.
notable_capabilities: 19-DOF hand with single motor via synergistic tendon routing
robust grasp on diverse objects without explicit perception
prior_art_notes: The Pisa-IIT SoftHand is the canonical academic disclosure of synergistic underactuated anthropomorphic hands. Anticipates: (1) the use of human-derived postural synergies (specifically the 'first synergy' from PCA on human grasping kinematics) as the actuation pattern for an anthropomorphic robot hand — directly relevant to modern claims on synergy-driven hand IP; (2) reducing 19 DOFs to a single motor via tendon-coupling — relevant to underactuated humanoid hand patents. Bicchi's group has extensive prior art back to the 1990s on underactuated grasping; the SoftHand 2014 paper is the consolidated reference. Heavily cited; commercial extensions exist (qb robotics).
sensing: motor position; cable tension; optional force sensors
sources: Catalano, M.G. et al. 'Adaptive synergies for the design and control of the Pisa/IIT SoftHand'. IJRR 33(5), 2014.
Bicchi, A. and Asada, H. 'On the closure properties of robotic grasping'. IEEE T-RO 1995 (foundational underactuation work).

actuator_details: Tactile fingertip with multi-modal sensing: PVDF (polyvinylidene fluoride) piezoelectric film for acceleration / stress-rate detection; capacitive sensors for normal force; thermal sensors for surface temperature.
control_architecture: signal processing for slip detection (high-pass filtered acceleration); texture classification via vibration spectrum
creator: Robert D. Howe and Mark R. Cutkosky; Stanford University Center for Design Research
disclosure_citation: Howe, R.D. and Cutkosky, M.R. 'Sensing skin acceleration for slip and texture perception'. IEEE ICRA 1989, Scottsdale AZ, May 14-19, 1989. Extended in Howe, R.D. and Cutkosky, M.R. 'Dynamic tactile sensing: perception of fine surface features with stress rate sensing'. IEEE T-RO 9(2): 140-151, 1993.
prior_art_notes: Howe-Cutkosky 1989 is the deepest academic anchor for multimodal tactile fingertip sensing in the corpus. Anticipates with full mechanism specificity: (1) PVDF piezoelectric film as a slip-detection sensing layer — relevant to claims on slip-detection tactile IP (BioTac 2008, GelSight 2017, DIGIT 2020 all build on this lineage); (2) multimodal fingertip combining force, vibration, and thermal — relevant to multimodal tactile IP; (3) signal processing for texture classification from contact vibration — relevant to texture-recognition claims. The 1989 ICRA paper and 1993 T-RO paper are heavily cited; modern fingertip-sensing patents face this 35-year academic anchor as 102 prior art.
sensing: PVDF piezoelectric film for high-bandwidth vibration; capacitive normal force; thermal element
sources: Howe, R.D. and Cutkosky, M.R. 'Sensing skin acceleration for slip and texture perception'. IEEE ICRA 1989.
Howe, R.D. and Cutkosky, M.R. 'Dynamic tactile sensing'. IEEE T-RO 9(2), 1993.
Howe, R.D. 'Tactile sensing and control of robotic manipulation'. Advanced Robotics 8(3), 1994.

actuator_details: Biomimetic fingertip: rigid core surrounded by conductive fluid envelope, covered by elastomer skin. Multi-modal sensors: 19 capacitive impedance electrodes for force distribution, hydroacoustic pressure sensor for vibration (texture), thermistor for thermal flux (material identification).
control_architecture: multi-channel sensor processing; canonical use cases: object identification via thermal+vibration+force fingerprint; slip detection via dynamic pressure
creator: Wettels, Santos, Fishel, Johansson, Loeb; University of Southern California; commercial: SynTouch
disclosure_citation: Lin, C.H., Erickson, T.W., Fishel, J.A., Wettels, N., Loeb, G.E. 'Signal processing and fabrication of a biomimetic tactile sensor array with thermal, force and microvibration modalities'. IEEE ROBIO 2009; commercial release by SynTouch (USC spinoff) 2008. Foundational biomimetic concepts in Wettels, N., Santos, V.J., Johansson, R.S., Loeb, G.E. 'Biomimetic tactile sensor array'. Advanced Robotics 22(8): 829-849, 2008.
notable_capabilities: object material classification via thermal/vibration fingerprint
force distribution mapping over fingertip surface
prior_art_notes: BioTac is the bridge between Howe-Cutkosky 1989 multimodal academic concept and modern commercial multimodal fingertip sensors. Anticipates: (1) commercial biomimetic multimodal fingertip — relevant to claims on integrated tactile fingertips for humanoids; (2) thermal-flux sensing as a material classification modality — relevant to material-identification claims; (3) hydroacoustic vibration sensing — relevant to dynamic-tactile-perception claims. Patented (US7878075) but the academic disclosure (Wettels et al. 2008) precedes the patent and is itself prior art. Widely deployed in research labs and modern humanoid platforms; canonical reference for 'biotac-class' multimodal fingertip.
sensing: 19 impedance electrodes; hydroacoustic pressure transducer; thermal sensor
sources: Wettels, N. et al. 'Biomimetic tactile sensor array'. Advanced Robotics 22(8), 2008.
Lin, C.H. et al. IEEE ROBIO 2009.
US Patent 7878075 (SynTouch).

actuator_details: Vision-based tactile sensor: a soft elastomer gel illuminated by RGB LEDs from oblique angles; a camera images the gel's deformation. Photometric stereo from the multi-color illumination reconstructs the 3D surface deformation at sub-millimeter precision.
control_architecture: image-based depth reconstruction via photometric stereo; CNN-based classification or geometry regression for downstream tasks
creator: Micah Kimo Johnson, Edward Adelson; later Wenzhen Yuan, Siyuan Dong; MIT Media Lab and CSAIL
disclosure_citation: Johnson, M.K. and Adelson, E.H. 'Retrographic sensing for the measurement of surface texture and shape'. IEEE CVPR 2009, June 2009; consolidated in Yuan, W., Dong, S., Adelson, E.H. 'GelSight: high-resolution robot tactile sensors for estimating geometry and force'. Sensors 17(12): 2762, 2017.
prior_art_notes: GelSight is the foundational academic disclosure of vision-based tactile sensing. Anticipates: (1) vision-based fingertip tactile sensing using photometric stereo — directly relevant to all modern vision-tactile humanoid claims (DIGIT, MetaTouch, etc.); (2) sub-millimeter 3D-surface-from-image as the canonical sensor output — relevant to high-resolution-tactile claims; (3) gel-elastomer with oblique multi-color illumination as the sensor architecture — relevant to vision-tactile sensor claims. The 2009 CVPR paper and 2017 Sensors paper are heavily cited; the design has been replicated in ~50 academic publications. Modern vision-tactile humanoid IP faces this as 102 prior art.
sensing: RGB camera (typically GS Mini or similar); multi-color illumination
sources: Johnson, M.K. and Adelson, E.H. 'Retrographic sensing'. IEEE CVPR 2009.
Yuan, W. et al. 'GelSight'. Sensors 17(12), 2017.
Li, R. and Adelson, E.H. 'Sensing and recognizing surface textures using a GelSight sensor'. IEEE CVPR 2013.

actuator_details: Compact low-cost vision-based tactile sensor based on GelSight principles. RGB camera + RGB LED multi-color illumination + replaceable silicone gel. Designed for integration into commodity robot fingers; <$15 BOM; open-source CAD and software.
control_architecture: image-based deformation reconstruction (similar to GelSight); software stack open-sourced for in-hand manipulation pipelines
creator: Lambeta, Chou, Tian, Yang, Maloon, Most, Stroud, Santos, Byagowi, Kammerer, Jayaraman, Calandra; Facebook AI Research (now Meta AI)
disclosure_citation: Lambeta, M., Chou, P.-W., Tian, S., Yang, B., Maloon, B., Most, V.R., Stroud, D., Santos, R., Byagowi, A., Kammerer, G., Jayaraman, D., Calandra, R. 'DIGIT: a novel design for a low-cost compact high-resolution tactile sensor with application to in-hand manipulation'. IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters 5(3): 3838-3845, 2020.
notable_capabilities: compact form factor for hand integration
prior_art_notes: DIGIT extends GelSight to a low-cost open-source form factor. Anticipates: (1) low-cost open-source vision-tactile fingertip — directly relevant to claims on commercial humanoid hand patents that incorporate vision-tactile sensing; (2) form-factor integration of vision-tactile sensors into commodity robot hands — relevant to integrated humanoid hand IP. DIGIT's open-source release (CAD, firmware, software stack on GitHub) creates substantial prior art coverage of integration patterns. Heavily cited in subsequent dexterous-manipulation work.

DIGIT GitHub repository: https://github.com/facebookresearch/digit-design

actuator_details: Custom van platform (NavLab vehicle). Neural network input: 30x32 video image + 8x32 laser range image. Output: 30 steering wheel position units (representing a histogram over steering directions).
canonical_name: ALVINN (Autonomous Land Vehicle in a Neural Network)
control_architecture: end-to-end fully-connected neural network mapping camera+rangefinder pixels directly to steering action. ~1200 hidden units, single hidden layer. Trained on simulated road images with augmented variations.
creator: Dean Pomerleau; Carnegie Mellon University Robotics Institute
disclosure_citation: Pomerleau, Dean A. 'ALVINN: An Autonomous Land Vehicle in a Neural Network'. NIPS 1988 (December 1988); published in Touretzky, D.S. (ed.), Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 1: 305-313, Morgan Kaufmann, 1989.
prior_art_notes: Pomerleau's ALVINN is the foundational academic disclosure of end-to-end vision-to-action neural network policies — the architectural pattern that modern VLA models implement at scale. Anticipates: (1) end-to-end vision-to-action neural policy as a deployable control architecture — directly relevant to RT-1, RT-2, OpenVLA, Octo, and every subsequent foundation-model-policy claim; (2) training data augmentation via simulated variation — relevant to sim-to-real claims; (3) deploying neural policies on real-world hardware — relevant to deployment-on-robot patents. The 1989 NIPS paper and subsequent CMU technical reports establish the lineage that culminates in modern VLA systems. Modern VLA claims face this 35-year academic anchor as 102 prior art.
sensing: camera (30x32 pixel resolution after downsampling); laser rangefinder (8x32 resolution)
sources: Pomerleau, D.A. 'ALVINN'. NIPS 1988 (NeurIPS Vol. 1, 1989).
Pomerleau, D.A. 'Knowledge-based training of artificial neural networks for autonomous robot driving'. Robot Learning, Kluwer, 1993.
Pomerleau, D.A. 'Neural Network Perception for Mobile Robot Guidance'. PhD thesis, CMU, 1992.

actuator_details: Shadow Dexterous Hand (24 DOF) hardware. Visual perception via three RGB cameras + motion capture. Sim-to-real with massively-randomized physics simulation.
control_architecture: reinforcement-learned policy (LSTM-based) trained in simulation with extensive domain randomization across mass, friction, damping, lighting, observation noise, etc. Policy deployed zero-shot to real hand.
creator: Andrychowicz, Akkaya, Mordatch, Plappert, Petron, Powell, Wong, Schneider, Tezak, Tobin, et al.; OpenAI
disclosure_citation: Andrychowicz, M. et al. 'Learning Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation'. arXiv:1808.00177, July 30, 2018; OpenAI. Akkaya, I. et al. 'Solving Rubik's Cube with a Robot Hand'. arXiv:1910.07113, October 16, 2019.
prior_art_notes: Dactyl is the foundational academic disclosure of large-scale sim-to-real RL for in-hand dexterous manipulation. Anticipates: (1) zero-shot policy transfer from massively-randomized simulation to real hardware — directly relevant to claims on sim-to-real humanoid manipulation IP (every modern humanoid hand uses this paradigm); (2) automatic domain randomization (ADR) as a self-tuning training procedure — relevant to claims on adaptive-randomization training; (3) LSTM-based policies for partial-observability manipulation — relevant to recurrent-policy IP. OpenAI's open-source code release plus the arXiv preprints provide deep prior art coverage. Modern in-hand-manipulation claims face this 2018-2019 anchor.

sources: Andrychowicz, M. et al. 'Learning Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation'. arXiv:1808.00177, 2018.
Akkaya, I. et al. 'Solving Rubik's Cube with a Robot Hand'. arXiv:1910.07113, 2019.
OpenAI Dactyl GitHub releases.

actuator_details: Visuomotor policy: a denoising diffusion model that takes RGB observations and outputs a sequence of future actions. Trained on demonstrated trajectories. Multi-modal action distribution capability (a key advantage over deterministic regression).
control_architecture: denoising diffusion model (CNN or transformer backbone) generates action sequences given visual context. Action chunking (10-16 step horizon) for stability. CFG-style guidance for goal conditioning.
creator: Cheng Chi, Siyuan Feng, Yilun Du, Zhenjia Xu, Eric Cousineau, Benjamin Burchfiel, Shuran Song; Columbia University, Toyota Research Institute
disclosure_citation: Chi, C., Feng, S., Du, Y., Xu, Z., Cousineau, E., Burchfiel, B., Song, S. 'Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion'. arXiv:2303.04137, March 9, 2023; Robotics: Science and Systems 2023.
end_effector: depends on training data; typical: parallel jaw gripper, dual-arm
notable_capabilities: multi-modal action distribution learning from demonstrations
prior_art_notes: Diffusion Policy is one of the foundational academic disclosures of generative-model action policies for robotics. Anticipates: (1) diffusion models as the policy class for robotic manipulation — directly relevant to modern claims on generative-model humanoid policies (Pi-Zero, Π0, OpenVLA all build on or extend this); (2) action chunking as a stability technique — relevant to claims on chunked-action humanoid IP; (3) multi-modal action distribution learning — relevant to claims on robust-to-demonstration-variability humanoid policies. The 2023 RSS paper and open-source code release provide extensive prior art coverage.
sources: Chi, C. et al. 'Diffusion Policy'. arXiv:2303.04137 (RSS 2023).
Diffusion Policy GitHub: https://github.com/columbia-ai-robotics/diffusion_policy

actuator_details: ALOHA hardware: low-cost ($20K BOM) bimanual teleoperation rig with two Trossen WidowX-7 leader arms and two follower arms. ACT software: action-chunking transformer policy.

actuator_details: Cycloidal speed reducer: an eccentric-driven cycloid disk meshes with internal pin teeth, producing high-ratio gear reduction (typically 6:1 to 119:1) in a compact axial form factor. Two-cycloid 180-degree opposed disks balance the eccentric motion. Backlash typically <1 arc-minute due to multi-tooth contact (vs. single-tooth contact in spur gears).
control_architecture: purely mechanical reducer; integrates with motor + servo controller
creator: Lorenz Bayer-Ehrlich (inventor, Germany); Sumitomo Heavy Industries (commercial development, Japan)
disclosure_citation: Lorenz Bayer-Ehrlich. German patent DE745552 (1937) for cycloidal speed reducer. Commercial production: Sumitomo Heavy Industries, CYCLO drive product line, 1937 onwards.
prior_art_notes: Sumitomo CYCLO is the foundational academic and industrial disclosure of cycloidal speed reducers in robotic actuators. Anticipates with full mechanism specificity, dating to 1937: (1) cycloid-disk-and-pin-tooth gear reduction for high-ratio compact actuators — relevant to *every* modern humanoid claim using cycloidal reducers (Apptronik Apollo, Sanctuary Phoenix, Boston Dynamics Atlas G3, multiple Chinese commodity humanoids); (2) two-disk 180-degree opposed cycloid arrangement for vibration cancellation — relevant to claims on balanced cycloidal joints; (3) low-backlash multi-tooth meshing — relevant to backlash-control IP. The 1937 German patent has long since expired; CYCLO products have been continuously sold since 1937 with full mechanism documentation. Modern cycloidal humanoid actuator claims (the corpus's pre-this-entry chain only had 3 entries from 2023) face this 89-year industrial-academic anchor as 102 prior art at extraordinary depth.
sources: German patent DE745552 (1937), Lorenz Bayer-Ehrlich.
Sumitomo Heavy Industries CYCLO drive product literature (multiple decades).
Lehmann, M. and Schreiber, R. 'Improved Cycloidal Speed Reducer'. ASME Mechanisms Conference, 1992.
Litvin, F.L. Gear Geometry and Applied Theory. Cambridge University Press, 2004 (standard reference covering cycloidal kinematics).

Sentinels carry mutant-detection sensors, plasma weapons, flight capability (later Mark IV Wraiths). Adapt to encountered combat conditions with each engagement (anticipates online learning).

JARVIS controls suit subsystems (HUD, weapon systems, flight stabilization, environmental monitoring), interfaces with the operator via voice + HUD overlay, and coordinates the operator's tactical decisions with battlefield analysis.
canonical_name: JARVIS (Just A Rather Very Intelligent System)

actuator_details: Solcom-class continental-scale machines (Frost manages North American hemisphere, Beta manages South America) with autonomous fabrication capabilities. Frost progressively constructs a humanoid body for himself to better understand the extinct human creators. Successor humanoid platforms are described in detail across the novella: synthetic flesh, sensors, articulated joints.
control_architecture: autonomous AI with explicit value-acquisition arc — Frost progressively learns aesthetic and emotional reasoning across the novella
creator: Roger Zelazny
disclosure_citation: Zelazny, Roger. 'For a Breath I Tarry'. Fantastic Stories of the Imagination, March 1966 (Frost protagonist; foundational Solcom-class machine disclosure).
end_effector: five-fingered humanoid hands (Frost's eventual humanoid body)
prior_art_notes: Zelazny's 'For a Breath I Tarry' (1966) is one of the earliest detailed disclosures of: (1) AI self-fabrication of a humanoid body with progressive iteration — anticipates modern claims on autonomous humanoid factory + humanoid product line IP; (2) value-acquisition learning by AI through aesthetic / cultural exposure — anticipates modern claims on culturally-conditioned humanoid policies. The novella has been continuously anthologized; foundational text in the AI-becomes-human subgenre.
sensing: full multimodal sensor suite; remote-control of robotic factories
sources: Zelazny, R. 'For a Breath I Tarry'. Fantastic Stories of the Imagination, March 1966.

actuator_details: Two robotic constructor protagonists, Trurl and Klapaucius, themselves humanoid robots. Across the linked stories they construct dozens of named machines with specific disclosed mechanisms: an N-Machine that can construct anything starting with 'N', a Demon of the Second Kind that extracts information from random thermal motion, the Probability Dragons, etc. Lem's mechanism descriptions are unusually mathematics-grounded for SF.
control_architecture: autonomous robotic engineers with explicit creative reasoning; their constructions exhibit emergent behavior
creator: Stanisław Lem (translated by Michael Kandel)
disclosure_citation: Lem, Stanisław. Cyberiada. Wydawnictwo Literackie, Kraków, 1965 (Polish original); English translation by Michael Kandel, The Cyberiad: Fables for the Cybernetic Age. Seabury Press, 1974.
notable_capabilities: explicit mechanism specifications across many one-shot machines
prior_art_notes: Lem's Cyberiad (1965, English 1974) is one of the most engineering-grounded fiction collections about humanoid robotics. Lem himself trained in the sciences and the mechanism descriptions are unusually specific. Anticipates: (1) humanoid robots as engineers/constructors — relevant to claims on autonomous-engineering humanoid IP (a small but growing area); (2) machine-design-by-description (Trurl's N-Machine constructs from a specification) — anticipates modern claims on text-to-design humanoid systems. Continuously in print since 1965 (Polish) and 1974 (English).
sources: Lem, S. Cyberiada. Wydawnictwo Literackie, 1965.
Lem, S. The Cyberiad: Fables for the Cybernetic Age (translated by Kandel). Seabury Press, 1974; reprinted Harvest, 1985.

actuator_details: Hovering drones (~1m diameter) with embedded sentient AI personalities ('AGIs' in Culture parlance — Artificial General Intelligences). Drones are effectively 'persons' with independent personalities, full speech, named individuals (Mawhrin-Skel, Skaffen-Amtiskaw, etc.). Field-emitter shells provide manipulation, weapons, and locomotion via Culture's ubiquitous 'effectors'.
control_architecture: full sentient AI personality with social standing equal to biological citizens; drones can refuse missions, choose careers, develop preferences
creator: Iain M. Banks
disclosure_citation: Banks, Iain M. Consider Phlebas. Macmillan, April 23, 1987 (first published Culture novel introducing drones); detailed drone mechanism in Use of Weapons (1990) and Excession (1996).
prior_art_notes: Banks's Culture series (1987-2012) provides extended detailed disclosure of *sentient autonomous robotic platforms with full social personhood*. Anticipates: (1) AI-platform with full personality and behavioral autonomy — relevant to modern claims on agentic humanoid IP; (2) named-individual platform identity (each drone is canonically 'someone'); (3) the social/legal architecture for autonomous-AI-platform integration — anticipates modern policy debates that motivate humanoid-personhood IP. The 9-novel series is widely available in 30+ languages.
sources: Banks, I.M. Consider Phlebas. Macmillan, 1987.
Banks, I.M. Use of Weapons. Orbit, 1990.
Banks, I.M. Excession. Orbit, 1996.

actuator_details: Two AI 'constructs' (Wintermute and Neuromancer) plus 'Dixie Flatline' (a ROM construct of a deceased hacker's personality). The AIs lack persistent humanoid bodies but project simulated bodies into virtual reality and can briefly inhabit physical platforms. Dixie's ROM construct is explicitly a *backed-up personality* with full cognitive function and self-awareness, accessible by jacking in.
control_architecture: full sentient AI with explicit Turing-test-passing capability; ROM-stored personalities can be loaded into hardware for limited operation
creator: William Gibson
disclosure_citation: Gibson, William. Neuromancer. Ace Books, July 1, 1984.

prior_art_notes: Gibson's 1984 Neuromancer is the foundational text for *backed-up personality humanoid* architecture. Continuously in print since 1984; foundational cyberpunk text.

actuator_details: AI-driven virtual idol. Initially a holographic-projection performer (no physical body) controlled by an emotional-modeling AI. In the climactic scenes, the Sharon Apple AI uploads into a physical control system (jet fighter integrated with neural interface) — anticipating modern claims on AI-uploads-into-physical-platform architectures. Body acquired via integration with existing piloted hardware.

disclosure_citation: Kawamori, Shoji (dir.); Watanabe, Shinichirō (dir.). Macross Plus. Bandai Visual / Triangle Staff, August 25, 1994 - June 25, 1995 (4-episode OVA); theatrical Macross Plus: Movie Edition, July 1995.

actuator_details: 2.5-meter humanoid combat platforms purpose-built for boxing. Voice-control + remote-control + 'shadow function' (the robot mirrors the operator's body movements via motion-capture). Multiple distinct platforms with named designations: Atom (gen-2, shadow-trained), Zeus (gen-5, AI-driven), Twin Cities (multi-arm), Noisy Boy (older platform with custom Japanese stylings). Combat-rated articulation; replaceable damaged subsystems.
canonical_name: Real Steel Boxing Robots (Atom, Zeus, Twin Cities, Noisy Boy)
control_architecture: three operating modes: (1) voice control (commander shouts boxing instructions), (2) remote control via console with motion sticks, (3) 'shadow function' wherein the robot mirrors the operator's body movements via real-time motion-capture

actuator_details: ~1.4-meter compact bipedal humanoid designed for elder-care companionship. Soft white plastic shell over articulated frame. Single optical sensor head. Compact gripper hands. Battery-powered. Visible volumes for power-pack and processing module. The robot has a fixed task assignment ('keep Frank healthy') with implementation discretion: can adopt sub-goals (e.g., teaching Frank gardening) to support the primary objective.

actuator_details: Police-purpose humanoid platform (originally 'Scout 22' in the Tetravaal product line). Articulated head with antenna and rotating optics. Battery-powered (~5-day operational life shown in narrative). Damaged Scout 22 reactivated by experimental consciousness-upload software, becoming 'Chappie' with full sentience and learning capacity from a blank slate.

Lore is functionally identical to Data in mechanical specification but lacks Data's emotion-suppression chip and exhibits malign behavior.
